docs.title: IBM Bob — OpenSlava Bobathon
docs.text: Welcome to the IBM Bob Hands-On Workshop at OpenSlava! This is your complete guide for the 90-minute session — choose a track, follow the step-by-step instructions, and build real applications with IBM Bob.

docs.title: Choose Your Track
docs.text:
• 🟢 Beginner

    ~70 min · 3 labs · No prior Bob experience needed

    Build a confetti welcome app, add layover support to a full-stack travel app, then wire up date pickers and a mock AI booking agent — touching Ask, Plan, and Agent modes throughout.

    Start Beginner Track

  • 🟡 Intermediate

    ~70 min · 2 labs · Basic Bob familiarity assumed

    Drive a full Issue → Branch → Code → PR loop with GitHub MCP, then author and commit version-controlled team rules that Bob applies automatically on every interaction.

    Start Intermediate Track

  • 🔴 Expert

    ~90 min · 4 labs · For power users and architects

    Discover a banking-industry codebase, build a React UI, run a security audit, author fintech compliance rules, create a custom scoped mode, and automate the full SDLC with GitHub MCP.

    Start Expert Track

  • 🏆 Challenge

    Open build · First 3 to finish win a prize

    Build PocketLedger — a full-stack personal finance tracker — using every Bob skill you've learned: /init, rules, a custom mode, and a complete GitHub issue-to-PR loop. All Bob artefacts are judged.

    Take the Challenge

docs.title: 1 — Get an IBMid
docs.text: IBM Bob requires an IBMid. IBMid is free — create one at ibm.com/account/reg (takes ~2 minutes). If you already have one, skip this step.

docs.title: 2 — Install IBM Bob
docs.text:
IBM Bob is a standalone IDE — not a VS Code extension. Download from bob.ibm.com/download and sign in with your IBMid.

IBM Bob IDE (recommended)Bob Shell (terminal)

Download the installer for your OS from bob.ibm.com/download:

OS Installer macOS (Apple Silicon) .pkg — mac-ARM macOS (Intel) .pkg — mac-intel Windows .exe Linux (Debian/Ubuntu) .deb Linux (Red Hat/Fedora) .rpm

Run the installer, follow the wizard, then sign in with your IBMid on first launch.

Prefer the terminal? Install Bob Shell instead:

macOS / Linux 

curl -fsSL https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.sh | bash
Windows (PowerShell) 
powershell -ep Bypass 'irm -Uri "https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.ps1" | iex'
Authenticate at bob.ibm.com/login when prompted.

  • Git configured with user.name and user.email

docs.title: OpenSlava — Beginner Track
docs.text: Three labs · ~70 minutes total · No prior Bob experience needed

docs.title: Track Overview
docs.text:
# Lab Time Goal B1 Explore Modes & Build the OpenSlava 2026 Welcome App 25 min Learn the three Bob modes by building a confetti welcome page B2 Connect & Expand Galaxium Travels: Flights with Layovers 25 min Add a real feature to a full-stack app using Ask → Plan → Agent B3 Date Picker, Price Ranker & Booking Agent 20 min Three quick enhancements showing Bob handling UI, logic, and mock AI

How to use this guide

Each lab builds on the previous one. Complete them in order. Every prompt block is copy-pasteable — click the copy icon on the top-right of any code block.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• IBM Bob IDE installed and signed in — download from bob.ibm.com/download (standalone app, not a VS Code extension), or Bob Shell if you prefer a terminal (curl -fsSL https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.sh | bash)
  • Node.js 20 LTS installed
  • Git installed
  • Galaxium repo cloned: git clone https://github.com/IBM/galaxium-travels

docs.title: Lab B1 — Explore Modes & Build the OpenSlava 2026 Welcome App
docs.text: 25 minutes · No code experience needed

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
The three Bob modes — Ask, Plan, and Agent — each have a distinct role. This lab makes the difference tangible by using all three to build a single small app.

docs.title: Why use three modes instead of just one?
docs.text:
Splitting work across modes is a smart development pattern, not just a Bob quirk. Each mode has different tool permissions by design:

  • Ask can read files but cannot write or run commands — safe for exploration and Q&A
  • Plan can read and propose changes but cannot execute — ideal for design without side-effects
  • Agent can read, write, and run commands — the full power of an autonomous coding agent

Using the right mode for each phase keeps Bob's actions predictable, reviewable, and reversible. When you prototype in Ask, nothing breaks. When you finalize in Agent, every action is intentional.

docs.title: Step 1 — Ask mode: understand the modes
docs.text:
1. Open IBM Bob on an empty folder
  2. Select Ask mode
  3. Send this prompt:
What are the three built-in Bob modes, what tools does each one permit,
and when should I use each?

Observe: Bob gives a clear answer but cannot create files or run commands. Ask mode is read-only by design — perfect for questions and exploration.

Ask mode = read-only

Ask mode has no edit or command tool groups. Bob can see your code but cannot touch it. This is the safest mode to use when you want answers without the risk of unintended changes.

docs.title: Step 2 — Plan mode: design the app
docs.text:
1. Switch to Plan mode in the sidebar
  2. Send this prompt:
Plan a React + Vite app called "OpenSlava 2026 Welcome".
It should show a full-screen welcome page with:
- Background colour IBM Bob blue (#0f62fe)
- White text: "Welcome to OpenSlava 2026"
- Subtitle: "Powered by IBM Bob"
- A confetti burst when the page loads

The confetti must use only CSS keyframe animations and vanilla JS — no npm packages.
Produce a component list, the CSS animation approach, and a file layout.

Observe: Bob produces a detailed plan — component names, CSS strategy, file tree — but writes nothing to disk. Plan mode can design but not implement.

Plan mode = design without side-effects

Plan mode can read and propose edits, but does not execute commands. Use it to pair-design with Bob before committing to an implementation. A good plan prompt saves you from costly mid-build pivots.

Why plan before building?

Asking Bob to plan first gives you a chance to review and refine the approach. If the plan looks off, you correct it here — not after Bob has written 15 files. This is the same discipline as writing a design doc before opening an editor.

docs.title: Step 3 — Agent mode: implement
docs.text:
1. Switch to Agent mode
  2. Send this prompt:
Implement the plan you just designed.
Scaffold a Vite + React app, create a WelcomeScreen component,
apply the IBM Bob blue colour scheme, and implement the confetti
using CSS keyframe animations on randomly positioned <span> elements
created by a small vanilla JS helper (no npm packages).

Observe:

  • Bob runs npm create vite, installs dependencies
  • Creates src/WelcomeScreen.tsx with the welcome layout
  • Creates src/confetti.ts — generates ~40 <span> elements with random colours, positions, rotation, and staggered CSS animation delays
  • Adds confetti CSS to src/index.css

Review Bob's tool calls before approving

Bob will ask permission before running commands like npm create vite. Read the proposed command before clicking Approve. This is the safest habit to build: understand what Bob is doing at every step. You can always edit a proposed command before approving it.

docs.title: Step 4 — Run it
docs.text:
npm run dev

Open http://localhost:5173 — confetti should burst on load.

Didn't get confetti?

Ask Bob in Agent mode: "The confetti isn't appearing — check confetti.ts and the CSS animation names match."

This is normal iterative development. First runs rarely work perfectly. Bob reads the error, diagnoses it, and fixes it — often in one message. The pattern is: run → observe → feed the error back → repeat.

docs.title: Step 5 — Reflection: start a new task
docs.text:
Switch back to Ask mode, click + New task to start a fresh conversation, and send:

What would have happened if I had tried to run npm install
in Ask or Plan mode?

Why start a new task?

Bob has a 270,000-token context window — a large but finite budget. Every file read, tool call, and response consumes tokens. Starting a new task with + New task gives you a clean slate for a new topic. The old conversation stays in history but no longer consumes your budget.

Best practice: Start a new task when you change topic, finish a build phase, or notice Bob starting to drift or contradict itself. Keep tasks focused and short.

docs.title: Lab B2 — Connect & Expand Galaxium Travels: Flights with Layovers
docs.text: 25 minutes · Requires Lab B1 complete

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: Galaxium Travels is the official IBM Bob demo app — a full-stack interplanetary booking system. You will run /init to give Bob deep context, then plan and implement a real feature across the full stack.

docs.title: Why /init matters
docs.text:
Large language models are stateless — each new conversation starts with zero memory of the codebase. Without explicit context, Bob must re-discover every file from scratch on every task, which wastes tokens and produces inconsistent results.

/init solves this by scanning the project and writing a structured AGENTS.md summary that Bob reads at the start of every conversation automatically. It is the equivalent of onboarding documentation for Bob — written once, applied everywhere.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Lab B1 complete (modes understood)
  • Python 3.8+ installed
  • Galaxium cloned: git clone https://github.com/IBM/galaxium-travels

docs.title: Step 1 — Clone and start
docs.text:
cd galaxium-travels
./start.sh

Open http://localhost:5173 — you should see the Galaxium flight booking UI.

Start.sh takes ~2 minutes

It installs Python deps, Node deps, and starts both servers. Frontend on :5173, backend on :8001.

docs.title: Step 2 — Run /init
docs.text:
1. Open the galaxium-travels/ folder in IBM Bob
  2. Switch to Agent mode
  3. Type /init and send

What happens: Bob reads the entire codebase, then writes:

  • AGENTS.md at the repo root — project overview, key constraints, file map
  • .bob/rules-agent/AGENTS-agent.md, .bob/rules-plan/AGENTS-plan.md, .bob/rules-ask/AGENTS-ask.md

Read AGENTS.md together. Bob has discovered:

  • The three services (frontend / backend / hold service)
  • Custom Tailwind tokens (space-dark, space-blue, cosmic-purple, …)
  • The FastMCP integration at /mcp
  • The key constraint: every new backend endpoint needs a REST handler AND a matching MCP tool

AGENTS.md — Bob's memory across sessions

Bob automatically injects AGENTS.md into every new conversation. This means:

  • New team members get project context instantly when they git clone and open Bob
  • You never repeat the same "here's how this project works" prompt
  • Rules and constraints discovered in one session carry forward to the next

Re-run /init whenever you add new modules, change directory structure, or onboard new team members.

You can edit AGENTS.md manually

The automated scan is a starting point. Add your own lines: deployment conventions, business rules, things the scan can't infer. Think of it as your team's living onboarding doc.

docs.title: Step 3 — Plan the layovers feature
docs.text:
Switch to Plan mode and send:

Plan a "flights with layovers" feature for Galaxium Travels.

A layover is a stop between the origin and final destination,
with a planet name and layover duration in minutes.

The feature needs:
1. A LayoverStop type added to the TypeScript types and Python models
2. FlightRoute updated to hold a list of layover stops (can be empty)
3. Price calculation that adds 10% per layover stop
4. An updated route card UI showing layover stops inline

Follow the existing AGENTS.md conventions.

Observe: Bob produces a plan across all three layers without writing a single file.

Always reference AGENTS.md conventions in your Plan prompts

Telling Bob to "follow the existing AGENTS.md conventions" is a powerful shorthand. Because AGENTS.md describes your project's patterns, Bob applies them automatically — naming conventions, file locations, required MCP tools alongside REST endpoints — without you having to repeat everything.

docs.title: Step 4 — Implement
docs.text:
Start a + New task and switch to Agent mode before sending this prompt. This keeps implementation context clean and separate from the planning discussion:

Implement the layovers plan. Follow the AGENTS.md conventions:
- Add the REST endpoint AND a matching MCP tool for any new backend route
- Use snake_case in Python, PascalCase for TypeScript types
- Use the existing Tailwind space tokens for any new UI elements

Observe Bob working across:

  • booking_system_backend/models.py — LayoverStop model
  • booking_system_backend/server.py — updated route schema, MCP tool registration
  • booking_system_frontend/src/types/ — LayoverStop TypeScript type
  • booking_system_frontend/src/pages/Flights.tsx — updated route card
  • A new LayoverBadge component

Restart the backend, refresh the browser — multi-stop routes now appear.

Why start a new task for implementation?

Starting a fresh task before the Agent implementation run keeps the planning discussion out of the implementation context. This prevents the model from trying to reconcile half-finished plans with the real files it is writing — a common cause of drift. Clean context → focused results.

docs.title: Step 5 — Verify
docs.text:
In Ask mode:

Does the new layover implementation follow the AGENTS.md constraint
that every backend route has both a REST handler and an MCP tool?

This is trust but verify — a healthy habit with any agentic tool. Ask mode can audit the codebase without risk of accidentally changing anything.

docs.title: Lab B3 — Date Picker, Price Ranker & Booking Agent
docs.text: 20 minutes · Requires Lab B2 complete · App must be running

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: Three quick enhancements showing Bob handling UI input, sorting logic, and a mock AI agent pattern — all without leaving the Galaxium codebase. Each enhancement shows a different Bob prompt technique.

docs.title: Enhancement 1 — Date picker (Agent mode)
docs.text:
Add a departure date picker to the Galaxium flight search form.
Use a native HTML <input type="date">.
When a date is selected, filter the search results client-side
to show only flights available on that day.
No external date library.

Why this prompt works: It is specific (native <input type="date">), states the constraint (no library), and describes the expected behaviour (filter on selection). Vague prompts like "add a date thing" produce inconsistent results. Be as specific as the input field on a well-designed form.

Verify the date input renders and the results list updates on selection.

docs.title: Enhancement 2 — Price sort toggle (Agent mode)
docs.text:
Add a sort toggle button to the Galaxium flight search results.
Clicking it cycles between "Price: Low to High" and "Price: High to Low".
Implement the sort entirely in component state — no external sort library.

Verify clicking the button re-orders the results.

Use @/path/to/file to give Bob precise context

If Bob needs context from a specific file, use @/booking_system_frontend/src/pages/Flights.tsx in your prompt instead of describing the file. Bob reads it directly. This is faster than pasting code and avoids copy-paste errors.

docs.title: Enhancement 3 — Interplanetary Booking Agent (Plan → Agent)
docs.text:
This enhancement follows the Plan → new task → Agent pattern deliberately — it is more complex and benefits from a design pass first.

First, switch to Plan mode:

Design a mock AI booking agent component called BookingAgent.
It takes a natural-language text input (e.g. "cheapest route to Europa")
and returns the top 3 matching routes from the existing flight data
using keyword matching and price/speed intent detection.
No real LLM call — pure client-side JavaScript logic.

Then click + New task, switch to Agent mode:

Implement the BookingAgent component you just planned.
- A text input + submit button
- Parse the input for destination keywords and "cheapest"/"fastest" intent
- Filter and rank the flights array accordingly
- Display the top 3 matching routes as cards

Test it: type "cheapest route to Europa" — the top 3 cheapest Europa flights should appear.

Ask Bob to explain it

Switch to Ask mode: "How does BookingAgent decide which flights match the intent 'cheapest'? Walk me through the logic."

This is great habit. Using Ask mode to review Agent's output helps you understand code Bob wrote — so you own it, not just run it.

docs.title: Key patterns from this track
docs.text: Pattern Why it matters Ask → Plan → Agent Each phase has the right permissions. Design without side-effects, then implement with confidence. Start a + New task between phases Clean context = focused results. Prevents planning drift from contaminating implementation. Run /init first on any new project Gives Bob persistent context without re-reading files every session. Re-run /init after major changes Keeps AGENTS.md current as the project grows. Review before approving Read every proposed command before clicking Approve. Bob can edit commands too. Be specific in prompts Name the file, the function, the constraint. Vague prompts produce vague code. Use @/file/path references Give Bob the exact file it needs rather than describing it.

docs.title: What's next?
docs.text: If you want to go deeper… Try Team standards and SDLC automation Intermediate Track Custom modes, MCP, and advanced Bob config Expert Track

docs.title: 🏆 OpenSlava — Final Challenge
docs.text: Open build · No time limit · First 3 to submit win a prize

docs.title: The Challenge
docs.text:
You have spent the last 90 minutes learning every dimension of IBM Bob — modes, /init, rules, custom modes, MCP, GitHub automation, and security auditing. Now put it all together in one coherent product, built entirely with Bob.

The first three participants to submit a passing pull request win a prize.

docs.title: Your Mission: PocketLedger
docs.text: Build PocketLedger — a personal finance tracker with a React frontend, a FastAPI backend, and a full Bob-powered development workflow baked in.

docs.title: Application description
docs.text: PocketLedger helps individuals track income and expenses. Users add transactions, see a live balance, and review a spending breakdown by category. The codebase must be clean, tested, and security-aware from the start — because you are going to use Bob to enforce that, not just hope for it.

docs.title: Feature list
docs.text: # Feature Layer F1 Add a transaction (amount, description, category, date) Backend + Frontend F2 List all transactions, newest first Backend + Frontend F3 Delete a transaction by ID Backend + Frontend F4 Live balance display (sum of all amounts, signed) Frontend F5 Spending breakdown by category (aggregated totals) Backend + Frontend F6 Simple bar chart for category totals (vanilla JS Canvas or SVG — no charting library) Frontend F7 Filter transactions by category via a dropdown Frontend F8 Data persisted to a SQLite database (no in-memory store) Backend F9 All API endpoints protected by a static bearer token (from environment variable) Backend F10 At least 5 unit tests covering the data layer Backend

docs.title: Technology constraints
docs.text:
• Backend: Python 3.11+ · FastAPI · SQLite (via sqlite3 or SQLAlchemy) · uvicorn
  • Frontend: React 18+ · Vite · plain CSS (no component library, no Tailwind)
  • No external charting libraries (Chart.js, D3, Recharts, etc.) for F6
  • Auth: static bearer token read from POCKETLEDGER_TOKEN env var — no OAuth, no sessions

docs.title: Bob Requirements
docs.text:
This is not just an application challenge — it is a Bob workflow challenge. Your submission must demonstrate that you used Bob correctly and completely. The following Bob artefacts are required and will be checked by the judges.

Why are Bob artefacts required?

The challenge is designed to test whether you can apply the full Bob development workflow, not just generate code quickly. Judges are looking for evidence that you:

  • Used /init to give Bob persistent project context
  • Created rules to enforce standards automatically (not just as prompts)
  • Built a custom mode with appropriate permission restrictions
  • Drove the full GitHub SDLC loop with MCP

A working app with no Bob artefacts scores zero. An app that demonstrates every Bob pattern — even if imperfect — scores high.

docs.title: B-REQ-1 — /init generated AGENTS.md
docs.text:
Run /init on the completed codebase. The AGENTS.md at the repo root must exist and must describe:

  • The two-service architecture (backend + frontend)
  • The auth model (bearer token from env)
  • The database layer
  • At least one project-specific constraint Bob inferred or that you added

When to run /init

Run /init after the project skeleton is in place — not on an empty folder. Then re-run it after you add a new module (e.g. when you add authentication). Each re-run refreshes Bob's map of the codebase.

You can also manually add constraints to AGENTS.md that Bob couldn't infer from the code: deployment notes, known limitations, team conventions. The judges will reward a well-curated AGENTS.md.

docs.title: B-REQ-2 — Team rules file
docs.text:
Create .bob/rules/pocketledger-standards.md containing at minimum these three rules:

All Python functions that handle monetary amounts must use float with exactly
2 decimal places of precision — never store raw user input directly to the DB.

All React components must have a JSDoc comment describing their props.

After every Agent mode interaction, append a one-line entry to bob-audit/audit.log
in the format: [ISO timestamp] [mode] [brief description of change]

Run at least one Agent mode interaction after creating the rules and confirm bob-audit/audit.log has a new entry.

Rules enforce standards without reminders

Once this rules file exists, Bob will:

  • Round monetary values automatically in every function it writes
  • Add JSDoc comments to every React component it creates
  • Append to bob-audit/audit.log after every Agent interaction

You don't need to ask. You don't need to remind Bob. The standard is always active. This is the difference between rules and prompts: rules are permanent, prompts are per-conversation.

docs.title: B-REQ-3 — Custom ledger-reviewer mode
docs.text:
Create .bob/custom_modes.yaml with a ledger-reviewer mode that:

  • Has read and mcp tool groups only (no edit, no command)
  • Has a roleDefinition describing it as a security-focused finance code reviewer
  • Has at least 3 customInstructions items covering: float precision, hardcoded secrets, and input validation

Use the mode to run at least one review prompt and include the output (copy it into a file ledger-review/initial-review.md in the repo).

Switch to your custom mode with a slash command

Once .bob/custom_modes.yaml is saved, type /ledger-reviewer in the chat to switch to it instantly. You don't need to navigate through the settings menu.

Why a read-only reviewer mode?

ledger-reviewer with no edit or command groups cannot modify your code, even if you ask it to. This enforced read-only constraint means you can run compliance reviews without any risk of unintended changes to your working code.

The output you save to ledger-review/initial-review.md becomes your project's first formal security review — committed to version control alongside the code it reviewed.

docs.title: B-REQ-4 — GitHub issue → PR loop
docs.text:
1. Push your repo to GitHub (public or private, your choice)
  2. Create a GitHub issue titled "Add CSV export for transactions" with a description of the feature
  3. Use Agent mode (with GitHub MCP) to read the issue, implement the endpoint, commit on a feature branch, and open a PR that references the issue number

The PR must exist on GitHub and must reference the issue. The CSV export endpoint does not need to be production-perfect — it just needs to exist and work for the basic case.

Use /create-pr for the PR step

After Bob has committed and pushed the feature branch, type /create-pr in the chat. Bob reads the git diff, identifies the linked issue from your branch name and commit message, generates a PR description, and creates the PR via GitHub MCP — all in one command.

Why issue → branch → PR, not just a direct commit?

The issue-to-PR loop creates a traceable link: requirement → implementation → review. This is the professional engineering workflow that works at scale.

When Bob reads the issue and generates a PR description that references #<issue-number>, GitHub automatically: - Links the PR to the issue - Closes the issue when the PR merges

The audit trail is automatic. This is what "Bob as a team tool" looks like in practice.

docs.title: How to submit
docs.text: When you are done, call over a facilitator — they will check your screen live.

docs.title: What the facilitator will check
docs.text: Check Pass criteria All 10 features (F1–F10) present Verified by running ./start.sh and testing the UI AGENTS.md exists and is non-trivial File present, >20 lines, describes architecture .bob/rules/pocketledger-standards.md exists File present, contains the 3 required rules bob-audit/audit.log has entries File present, at least 1 entry .bob/custom_modes.yaml defines ledger-reviewer Mode present, read-only groups only ledger-review/initial-review.md present File present, non-empty GitHub PR references the issue PR description contains #<issue-number> Tests pass pytest exits 0 in the backend directory

docs.title: Scoring tiebreaker
docs.text: If multiple submissions arrive at the same time, the tiebreaker is quality of AGENTS.md — specifically how well Bob was guided to capture the real architectural decisions of the project.

docs.title: Recommended workflow
docs.text:
Following the patterns you learned in the tracks will get you to a submission faster than guessing. Here is the recommended sequence:

%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#1a56db', 'primaryTextColor': '#ffffff', 'primaryBorderColor': '#1a56db', 'lineColor': '#6b7280', 'mainBkg': '#1a56db', 'nodeBorder': '#1a56db', 'clusterBkg': '#1e3a5f', 'titleColor': '#ffffff', 'edgeLabelBackground': 'transparent'}}}%%
flowchart TD
    A["📋 Plan mode\nDesign full project structure"] --> B["⚙️ Agent mode\nScaffold backend + frontend"]
    B --> C["🔧 /init\nGenerate AGENTS.md"]
    C --> D["📝 Create .bob/rules/\npocketledger-standards.md"]
    D --> E["⚙️ Agent mode\nBuild features F1–F10\n(+ New task between features)"]
    E --> F["🏦 Create ledger-reviewer mode\nRun review → save to file"]
    F --> G["🔁 Re-run /init\nUpdate AGENTS.md"]
    G --> H["🔀 GitHub MCP\nIssue → implement → /create-pr"]
    classDef node fill:#1a56db,color:#fff,stroke:#1a56db
    class A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H node

Start new tasks frequently

Each feature (F1 through F10) should ideally be its own Bob task. Clean context per feature means:

  • Bob focuses only on the feature at hand
  • Errors in one feature don't contaminate the next
  • The token budget stays healthy throughout

If you try to build all 10 features in a single conversation, the context window will fill and quality will degrade by F7.

docs.title: Hints & Guidance
docs.text:
These hints are here if you get stuck. Try without them first.

Hint 1 — Recommended start sequence
  1. Create an empty folder pocketledger/
  2. Open it in IBM Bob, switch to Plan mode, paste the feature list and ask Bob to design the full project structure
  3. Start a + New task, switch to Agent mode, scaffold both services
  4. Run /init once the skeleton is in place
  5. Create your rules file before writing any business logic
  6. Build features F1–F10 in Agent mode, one or two features per task
Hint 2 — Bearer token pattern (FastAPI) 

from fastapi import Header, HTTPException
import os

def verify_token(authorization: str = Header(...)):
    expected = f"Bearer {os.environ['POCKETLEDGER_TOKEN']}"
    if authorization != expected:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail="Unauthorized")
Add Depends(verify_token) to every route that should be protected.

The token is read from the environment — never hardcoded. If Bob ever hardcodes a token value, ask it to move the value to .env and load it with os.environ.

Hint 3 — Vanilla JS bar chart approach

Ask Bob in Plan mode first: 

Design a vanilla JS bar chart using the Canvas API that takes an array of
{ category: string, total: number } objects and renders horizontal bars.
No external library.
Then start a + New task and switch to Agent mode to implement.

The Plan → new task → Agent pattern is particularly important here because the chart logic is complex enough to benefit from a design pass.

Hint 4 — start.sh template

Your repo should include a start.sh at the root that starts both services so judges can run it easily: 

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -e
export POCKETLEDGER_TOKEN="${POCKETLEDGER_TOKEN:-dev-token-123}"
cd backend && pip install -r requirements.txt -q && uvicorn main:app --reload --port 8000 &
cd ../frontend && npm install -q && npm run dev &
wait

Hint 5 — GitHub MCP PR prompt 

Read GitHub issue #<number> from this repo.
Create a branch called feature/csv-export.
Implement a GET /transactions/export endpoint in main.py that returns
a CSV with columns: id, date, description, category, amount.
Use Python's built-in csv module.
Commit the change and open a pull request referencing the issue.
Then in the same chat type /create-pr to trigger the PR workflow.

Hint 6 — Context hygiene during the build

If Bob starts giving inconsistent responses or producing code that doesn't match your existing files:

  1. Start a + New task
  2. Reference your key files directly: @/backend/main.py @/frontend/src/App.tsx
  3. Remind Bob of the AGENTS.md conventions: "Follow the AGENTS.md conventions in this project"

Clean context is the single most effective fix for drift. Don't try to correct Bob in a long conversation — reset and start fresh.

docs.title: Prize
docs.text:
The first 3 participants to submit a passing pull request receive an IBM Bob prize. 🏆

Good luck — and enjoy building with Bob.

docs.title: OpenSlava — Expert Track
docs.text: Four labs · ~90 minutes total · For experienced Bob users

docs.title: Track Overview
docs.text: # Lab Time Goal E1 GFM Bank: Architecture, React UI & Security Audit 25 min Three-part banking lab — understand, build, and secure E2 /init, Re-Init & Fintech Rules 20 min Deep dive into /init and production-grade rules authoring E3 Custom Mode, Mode-Scoped Rules & Re-Init 20 min Build a read-only fintech-reviewer mode with PCI-DSS rules E4 GitHub MCP Integration 25 min Issue → branch → implement → PR driven entirely by Bob with GitHub MCP

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• IBM Bob IDE installed and signed in — download from bob.ibm.com/download (standalone app, not a VS Code extension), or Bob Shell if you prefer a terminal (curl -fsSL https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.sh | bash)
  • Python 3.11+ and Node.js 20 LTS installed
  • Git configured with user.name and user.email
  • GitHub account with a personal access token (repo scope) — needed for E4
  • GitHub MCP installed in Bob — needed for E4

docs.title: Lab E1 — GFM Bank: Architecture, React UI & Security Audit
docs.text: 25 minutes

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
The GFM Bank lab is an industry-grade demo with a Python/FastAPI backend, a teller CLI, a back-office CLI, and a deliberately vulnerable data pipeline. This lab runs all three parts in compressed form.

The three parts map directly to three Bob modes and three patterns you should carry into every real project:

  1. Ask for architecture discovery — understand before you build
  2. Agent for rapid UI scaffolding — Bob as a full-stack pair programmer
  3. Agent for security audit — systematic vulnerability analysis, not just guesswork

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1 — Clone the workshop repo (skip if you already have it)

git clone git@github-halvoribm:HalvorIBM/openslava.git
cd openslava

2 — Start the GFM Bank API

cd expert/labs/banking-industry/gfm-bank
./start.sh

API running at http://127.0.0.1:8000 · Docs at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs

Why localhost, not 0.0.0.0?

Notice the API binds to 127.0.0.1 — not all interfaces. This is a security best practice: development services should never be exposed on all network interfaces. The same rule applies to any service Bob scaffolds for you. If Bob suggests 0.0.0.0, change it before running.

Test credentials:

User Password Role teller teller123 TELLER backoffice backoffice123 BACKOFFICE

Sample IBAN: DE89545769475769453536 (Alice Müller)

docs.title: Part 1 — Architecture Understanding (8 min)
docs.text:
Open expert/labs/banking-industry/gfm-bank/ in IBM Bob. Switch to Ask mode:

Analyse the GFM Bank codebase (demo_api.py, teller_client.py, backoffice_client.py).
Explain the architecture, the role-based access model, and the transaction processing logic.
Create a Mermaid diagram showing the system components and a sequence diagram for a money transfer.

Why Ask mode for architecture discovery?

You are using Ask mode because you want to understand the system, not change it. Ask mode is read-only — Bob can read every file and reason about the full codebase, but cannot accidentally modify anything while exploring.

This is the professional pattern before any major work on an unfamiliar codebase: understand first, then plan, then implement. Using Ask mode enforces this discipline at the tool level.

Notice how Bob can produce a Mermaid diagram from code it reads — this is architecture documentation generated automatically from the source of truth, not a stale diagram someone drew once and never updated.

docs.title: Part 2 — Build the React Teller UI (10 min)
docs.text:
Switch to Agent mode. Start a + New task first — you are switching from discovery to implementation:

Build a React + Vite teller front-end for GFM Bank connected to http://127.0.0.1:8000.
Include: login form (credentials from .env), server health indicator, balance inquiry,
transaction history, money transfer form, and overdraft request message.
Plain CSS — no external component library.

Load credentials from .env, not hardcoded

The prompt explicitly says "credentials from .env". This is intentional — never hardcode passwords or tokens in source code. Bob follows this instruction and generates a .env file pattern.

If Bob proposes hardcoded credentials anywhere, correct it: "Move these credentials to a .env file and load them with import.meta.env in Vite".

Reference the API spec as context

The GFM Bank API has Swagger docs at http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs. You can reference this as context by adding @http://127.0.0.1:8000/openapi.json in your prompt — Bob fetches the OpenAPI spec and uses the exact endpoint shapes. This produces accurate API client code without trial and error.

docs.title: Part 3 — Security Audit (7 min)
docs.text:
Open expert/labs/banking-industry/security-audit/code/ in IBM Bob. Start a + New task and switch to Agent mode:

Analyse data_pipeline.py and synthetic_generator.py for security vulnerabilities.
For each finding provide: file, line, CWE category, severity, attack scenario,
and remediation recommendation.
Then generate SECURITY_AUDIT_REPORT.md.

Expected findings

Bob should find at minimum: hardcoded credentials, SQL injection, command injection, insecure pickle deserialization, disabled SSL, and MD5 password hashing. A total of 12 vulnerabilities across both files.

Why generate SECURITY_AUDIT_REPORT.md?

Asking Bob to write a structured audit report is a smart documentation pattern. The output:

  • Is immediately shareable with a security team
  • Traces each finding to a specific file and line
  • Includes CWE categories — machine-readable vulnerability identifiers used by security tooling
  • Persists across sessions (it is a file, not a chat message)

In a real project, you would commit this report and reference it in your PR. The finding is now tracked, not buried in a chat transcript.

docs.title: Lab E2 — /init, Re-Init & Fintech Rules
docs.text: 20 minutes · Requires E1 complete

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: /init reverse-engineers your codebase into a living AGENTS.md — Bob's persistent context document. Re-running it after adding modules updates that context. Rules let you encode compliance standards that Bob enforces automatically.

docs.title: The stateless problem at scale
docs.text:
In a 50-file banking application, asking Bob to discover the codebase fresh in every conversation wastes tokens and produces inconsistent results. Without context, Bob might:

  • Use float for monetary values (losing precision)
  • Miss the auth pattern used by existing endpoints
  • Add a REST endpoint without the required MCP tool counterpart

/init solves this by writing Bob's understanding of the project to disk, where it persists across every conversation and every team member's machine. Rules go further: they encode the invariants Bob must never violate, regardless of who is prompting or what they ask for.

docs.title: Step 1 — Run /init
docs.text:
From expert/labs/banking-industry/gfm-bank/, switch to Agent mode, type /init and send.

Read AGENTS.md:

  • What did Bob infer about the project structure?
  • What frameworks and patterns did it identify?
  • What constraints did it record (e.g. Decimal for monetary values)?

Open .bob/rules-agent/AGENTS-agent.md: compare to the root file. What is mode-specific?

Mode-specific AGENTS.md files

/init generates four context files:

  • AGENTS.md — root, loaded in all modes
  • .bob/rules-agent/AGENTS-agent.md — extra context for Agent (file structure, implementation patterns)
  • .bob/rules-plan/AGENTS-plan.md — extra context for Plan (architecture, constraints)
  • .bob/rules-ask/AGENTS-ask.md — extra context for Ask (project overview, glossary)

Each mode gets the context relevant to its purpose. Plan mode gets architecture guidance; Agent mode gets file layout and naming conventions.

docs.title: Step 2 — Author fintech rules
docs.text:
Create .bob/rules/fintech-standards.md:

All Python functions that handle monetary values must use the Decimal type, never float.

After every Bob interaction, append a one-line audit entry to bob-audit/audit.log
in the format: [ISO timestamp] [mode] [brief description of change]

Why Decimal over float?

This is a real production rule used in fintech systems. IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic accumulates rounding errors that are unacceptable for financial calculations. 0.1 + 0.2 in Python float is 0.30000000000000004 — not 0.3. For a bank, that is a compliance issue.

Encoding this as a Bob rule means Bob enforces it automatically on every function it writes or modifies — no code review step required to catch it.

The audit log pattern

The audit log rule creates a machine-readable trail of every Bob action. In regulated environments, you need to be able to answer: "on this date, what did the AI assistant change?" The bob-audit/audit.log file answers that question directly.

Commit this log alongside your code for a complete development history.

docs.title: Step 3 — Test the rules
docs.text:
In Agent mode:

Add a function called calculate_transfer_fee to demo_api.py
that calculates a 0.1% fee on a transfer amount and returns the fee value.

Observe:

  • Bob uses Decimal for the calculation automatically
  • bob-audit/audit.log has a new entry

docs.title: Step 4 — Add a module and re-init
docs.text:
In Agent mode:

Add a notifications/ module with a send_alert(event: str, account_id: str) function
that logs a structured alert message.

Re-run /init. Open AGENTS.md — observe notifications/ now appears in the codebase context.

Re-init after major structure changes

/init is not a one-time setup — it should be re-run whenever the project structure meaningfully changes:

  • After adding a new service or module
  • After a major refactor
  • When onboarding a new team member
  • Before a significant feature build

Think of it as "refresh Bob's map of the codebase". Old AGENTS.md with stale paths leads to Bob guessing at file locations — always re-init when in doubt.

docs.title: Step 5 — Commit
docs.text:
git add . && git commit -m "Add fintech Bob rules and updated AGENTS.md"

Always commit .bob/ alongside your code

Your Bob configuration is part of the project. Committing .bob/rules/, .bob/custom_modes.yaml, and AGENTS.md means:

  • New team members get the full Bob setup on git clone
  • Rule changes are code-reviewed like any other change
  • The history of what Bob was configured to do is auditable

docs.title: Lab E3 — Custom Mode, Mode-Scoped Rules & Re-Init
docs.text: 20 minutes · Requires E2 complete

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: Custom modes let you create role-specific Bob personas with their own tool restrictions and auto-injected instructions. A fintech-reviewer mode that can only read and report — never edit — is a powerful compliance tool.

docs.title: Why custom modes exist
docs.text:
The three built-in modes (Ask, Plan, Agent) cover the development workflow. But real teams have additional workflows that don't fit neatly into "implement" or "review":

  • A compliance reviewer who should never accidentally modify production code
  • A security auditor who needs to check for specific vulnerability classes systematically
  • A documentation writer who only updates .md files and never touches source code

Custom modes let you encode these roles with enforced tool permissions. The restrictions are at the tool level — they cannot be overridden by a clever prompt. If a mode lacks edit, Bob physically cannot write files, no matter what anyone asks.

docs.title: Step 1 — Create the custom mode
docs.text:
Open Bob Settings → Modes → Edit Project Modes (.bob/custom_modes.yaml).

Add the following complete mode definition:

customModes:
  - slug: fintech-reviewer
    name: 🏦 Fintech Reviewer
    roleDefinition: >-
      You are a senior fintech code reviewer specialising in PCI-DSS compliance,
      Python Decimal correctness, and secure API design.
      You analyse code for correctness, security, and regulatory compliance.
      You never modify files — you only report findings.
    whenToUse: >-
      Use this mode to review banking application code for compliance
      and quality issues without risk of accidental changes.
    customInstructions: |-
      - Always check for float usage where Decimal is required in monetary calculations
      - Flag any hardcoded secrets, API keys, or credentials
      - Check that all user inputs are validated server-side
      - Verify error messages do not expose stack traces or internal paths
      - Output findings as a numbered list with severity: Critical / High / Medium / Low
    groups:
      - read
      - mcp
      - skill

Why read, mcp, skill only?

Omitting edit and command makes this a read-only mode. Bob can analyse files and call MCP tools (e.g. to look up CVEs), but cannot write files or run commands. This is enforced at the tool-permission level — it cannot be overridden by a prompt.

This is the key security property of custom modes: the restriction is structural, not advisory. You cannot accidentally break it by typing "just fix it while you're there".

The slug becomes a slash command

Once you create a mode with slug: fintech-reviewer, you can switch to it instantly by typing /fintech-reviewer in the chat. No menu navigation needed. Custom mode slugs become first-class slash commands automatically.

Where to save the YAML file

  • .bob/custom_modes.yaml — project-scoped, committed to the repo, shared with the team ✅
  • ~/.bob/custom_modes.yaml — global, applies to all your workspaces

For compliance roles that are project-specific, always use the project-scoped file. For personal productivity modes you use across all projects, use the global file.

docs.title: Step 2 — Mode-scoped rules
docs.text:
Create .bob/rules-fintech-reviewer/01-pci-checklist.md:

When reviewing, always check these PCI-DSS items:

1. No card numbers, CVVs, or PINs logged or stored in plaintext
2. All API endpoints require authentication
3. Error messages do not reveal stack traces or internal file paths
4. All dependencies are on vendor-supported versions
5. Secrets and credentials are not hardcoded or committed to version control

Mode-scoped rules for the custom mode

The directory name must match the mode slug: .bob/rules-fintech-reviewer/. Bob injects these rules only when that mode is active — so the PCI-DSS checklist runs automatically every time a review is started, without anyone having to remember to include it.

This is systematic compliance review, not best-effort. The checklist is always present, always complete.

docs.title: Step 3 — Test the mode
docs.text:
1. Switch to 🏦 Fintech Reviewer mode in the Bob sidebar (or type /fintech-reviewer)
  2. Send:
Review the payments module (demo_api.py and data_pipeline.py)
for compliance issues.

Observe:

  • Bob reports a numbered finding list with severities
  • If you ask "Fix the SQL injection in data_pipeline.py", Bob refuses — it has no edit tools

Pair the reviewer mode with an Agent task

A good workflow: run fintech-reviewer to get the finding list, then start a new Agent mode task and reference the findings: "Fix findings 1, 3, and 5 from the fintech review." The reviewer can't write, the agent can't see your restrictions — each mode does exactly one job.

docs.title: Step 4 — Re-init and commit
docs.text:
Switch back to Agent mode. Re-run /init — the new custom mode now appears in AGENTS.md.

git add .bob/ && git commit -m "Add fintech-reviewer custom mode and PCI-DSS review checklist"

Re-init after adding custom modes

When you add a custom mode, re-running /init updates AGENTS.md to document the mode — its purpose, tool groups, and when to use it. This means:

  • New team members can discover the mode from AGENTS.md
  • Bob in any mode knows the fintech-reviewer mode exists and can suggest switching to it

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
In Ask mode:

How do custom modes, rules, and MCP servers differ as Bob extension mechanisms?
When would you use each one?

Three extension mechanisms — when to use each

Mechanism What it does Best for Rules Injects instructions into every conversation Coding standards, output formats, audit logging Custom modes Creates a new persona with restricted tool access Compliance roles, specialist reviewers, safe read-only workflows MCP servers Connects Bob to external systems GitHub, Jira, Datadog, Vault — anything outside your filesystem

They compose: a fintech-reviewer mode (custom mode) with PCI rules (rules) that calls a CVE database (MCP) is a complete compliance workflow built from three primitives.

docs.title: Lab E4 — GitHub MCP Integration
docs.text: 25 minutes · Requires E3 complete · GitHub account + PAT required

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text: MCP servers extend Bob with real-world integrations. GitHub MCP lets Bob read issues, create branches, commit code, and open PRs as native Bob actions — no shell scripts, no copy-paste.

docs.title: Why this matters in a regulated codebase
docs.text:
In financial software, the audit trail is not optional. Every change must be traceable:

  • Why was this change made? (Issue reference)
  • What was changed? (PR diff)
  • Who authorized it? (PR review)
  • When did it happen? (commit timestamp)

Bob with GitHub MCP produces all four automatically. The issue description becomes the requirement. The PR description links to the issue. The commit timestamp is git. The review is your team's normal process. Bob handles the mechanical linkage so nothing falls through the cracks.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install GitHub MCP (if not done in Intermediate track)
docs.text:
1. Bob sidebar → Marketplace → search GitHub → Install
  2. Settings → MCP → GitHub → set GITHUB_TOKEN (needs repo scope)
  3. Verify: no error badge; Bob shows GitHub tools in the sidebar

Push your banking lab to GitHub first

cd expert/labs/banking-industry/gfm-bank
git init && git add . && git commit -m "Initial GFM Bank commit"
gh repo create gfm-bank --public --source=. --push
Or use any repo you already have on GitHub.

Commit your .bob/ configuration before pushing

The rules and custom modes you built in E2 and E3 should be committed before you push: 

git add .bob/ AGENTS.md && git commit -m "Add Bob configuration: fintech rules and custom modes"
Anyone who clones your repo now gets the full Bob setup — context, standards, and compliance modes — immediately.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create a GitHub issue with Bob
docs.text:
In Agent mode:

Use GitHub MCP to create a new issue in this repo titled
"Add transaction export to CSV endpoint"
with label "enhancement" and body:
"Users need to download their transaction history as a CSV file.
The endpoint should accept an account_id parameter and return
a CSV with columns: date, amount, type."

Observe: Bob calls the GitHub MCP create_issue tool. Verify the issue appears on GitHub.

Write precise issue bodies

The quality of Bob's implementation is directly proportional to the quality of the issue body. A precise issue with column names, parameter names, and expected behaviour produces accurate code on the first pass. Vague issues ("add CSV export") produce vague implementations that require multiple correction rounds.

This is the same discipline as writing a good acceptance criterion — it benefits both human developers and AI agents equally.

docs.title: Step 3 — Issue-to-PR loop
docs.text:
Start a + New task in Bob (Agent mode):

Read the issue you just created.
Create a feature branch called "feature/csv-export".
Implement a GET /transactions/{account_id}/export endpoint in demo_api.py
that returns a CSV response (Content-Type: text/csv) with columns:
booking_ts, amount_eur, type.
Commit the change and open a pull request with a description referencing the issue number.

Observe Bob:

  1. Reads the issue via get_issue MCP tool
  2. Creates the branch via create_branch
  3. Implements the endpoint in demo_api.py
  4. Commits and pushes via create_or_update_file or push_files
  5. Opens a PR via create_pull_request referencing #<issue-number>

Watch the MCP tool calls in the approval panel

Each GitHub MCP tool call appears as an approval prompt — create_branch, create_or_update_file, create_pull_request. Review them before approving. You can see exactly what branch name Bob chose, what the commit message says, and what the PR description looks like — before any of it happens on GitHub.

This is the propose, then approve pattern at work on a remote system.

docs.title: Step 4 — Verify the endpoint
docs.text:
Test the new export endpoint with the sample IBAN DE89545769475769453536.
Show me the CSV output.

docs.title: Discussion questions
docs.text:
• What other MCP servers would fit this banking domain? (Jira, PagerDuty, Datadog, Vault)
  • How does GitHub MCP differ from Bob rules as an extension mechanism?
  • When should you use a custom mode vs. a rule vs. an MCP server?

Suggested answers for discussion

  • Jira MCP — same issue-to-PR pattern for teams not on GitHub
  • Vault MCP — Bob could rotate and reference secrets without ever seeing plaintext values
  • Datadog MCP — Bob could read production alerts and implement fixes without leaving the editor
  • Rules are project-internal standards. MCP servers connect to external systems. Custom modes restrict what Bob is allowed to do. All three compose cleanly.

docs.title: Bob extension mechanisms — comparison
docs.text: Mechanism Scope Modifies files? Requires setup? Version-controlled? Rules Per-project or per-mode No (informs Bob) Create .bob/rules/*.md Yes — commit .bob/ Custom modes Per-project or global No (restricts tools) Edit .bob/custom_modes.yaml Yes — commit .bob/ MCP servers Per-workspace Yes (via Bob actions) Install from Marketplace + token .bob/mcp.json for project scope /init Per-project Yes (writes AGENTS.md) Run once, re-run after changes Yes — commit AGENTS.md

docs.title: Mode tool groups reference
docs.text: Group What it allows read Read files, search codebase edit Create and modify files command Run shell commands mcp Use installed MCP servers skill Use installed skills browser Web browsing subtask Spawn subtasks

docs.title: Context hygiene reference
docs.text: Signal Action You are switching from planning to implementation Start + New task Bob starts contradicting earlier responses Start + New task The token counter is > 60% full Start + New task You added a new module or service Re-run /init You are onboarding a new team member Re-run /init + ensure .bob/ is committed You changed a rule and want it active now Start + New task (rules load on task start)

docs.title: OpenSlava — Intermediate Track
docs.text: Two labs · ~70 minutes total · Assumes basic Bob familiarity

docs.title: Track Overview
docs.text: # Lab Time Goal I1 GitHub SDLC with Bob 40 min Drive a full issue → branch → implement → PR loop with GitHub MCP I2 Author, Modify & Commit Rules 30 min Build version-controlled team standards that Bob applies automatically

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• IBM Bob IDE installed and signed in — download from bob.ibm.com/download (standalone app, not a VS Code extension), or Bob Shell if you prefer a terminal (curl -fsSL https://bob.ibm.com/download/bobshell.sh | bash)
  • Git configured (git config --global user.name and user.email)
  • GitHub account with a personal access token (repo scope)
  • GitHub MCP installed in Bob (see Lab I1 Step 1)

docs.title: Lab I1 — GitHub SDLC with Bob
docs.text: 40 minutes

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
Bob can drive an entire software development lifecycle — reading a GitHub issue, creating a branch, implementing the change, running validation, and opening a PR — without you leaving your editor. This lab shows you how, and more importantly, why this is valuable.

%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#1a56db', 'primaryTextColor': '#ffffff', 'primaryBorderColor': '#1a56db', 'lineColor': '#6b7280', 'mainBkg': '#1a56db', 'nodeBorder': '#1a56db', 'clusterBkg': '#1e3a5f', 'titleColor': '#ffffff', 'edgeLabelBackground': 'transparent'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    I["📋 GitHub Issue
(read via MCP)"] --> B["🌿 Feature Branch
(created by Bob)"] --> C["⚙️ Implement
(Agent mode)"] --> T["✅ Validate
(lint + tests)"] --> PR["🔀 Pull Request
(opened by Bob)"]
    classDef node fill:#1a56db,color:#fff,stroke:#1a56db
    class I,B,C,T,PR node

docs.title: Why MCP matters for SDLC
docs.text:
MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers extend Bob with real-world integrations. Without MCP, Bob can only interact with your local filesystem. With GitHub MCP, Bob can:

  • Read and create issues
  • Create branches
  • Commit and push files
  • Open pull requests — with a description that references the issue number

This turns Bob from a local coding assistant into a connected engineering agent that works within your team's actual workflow. Issues stay linked to implementations, PRs reference requirements, and the audit trail is automatic.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install GitHub MCP
docs.text:
1. Open the Bob sidebar → Marketplace icon
  2. Search for GitHub
  3. Click Install
  4. Open Bob settings → MCP → GitHub → set GITHUB_TOKEN to your personal access token (repo scope)
  5. Verify: no red error badge on the MCP server entry; Bob sidebar shows GitHub tools available

Create a token

GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Tokens (classic) → New token → tick repo → Generate.

Why use /configure-mcp in the chat?

You can also type /configure-mcp in Bob's chat to open the MCP configuration panel directly without leaving your conversation. This is especially useful mid-task when you realise you need a new integration.

MCP configuration can live at two levels: - Global (~/.bob/mcp_settings.json) — available in all workspaces - Project (.bob/mcp.json) — scoped to this repo, can be committed for team use

For team projects, committing .bob/mcp.json means everyone who clones the repo gets the same MCP configuration automatically.

docs.title: Step 2 — Open the lab repo in IBM Bob
docs.text:
cd intermediate/labs/github-sdlc

Open this folder in IBM Bob. It contains a React finance app skeleton and supporting docs.

docs.title: Step 3 — Plan and build the finance dashboard
docs.text:
Switch to Agent mode. Start by having Bob understand the project and plan the build:

Review this repository and propose a build plan for a small React finance dashboard application.
The app should use Yahoo Finance data for:
- Euro Stoxx 50 (`^STOXX50E`), DAX (`^GDAXI`), Nikkei 225 (`^N225`),
  Dow Jones Industrial Average (`^DJI`), and MSCI World (`URTH`).
The dashboard should provide views for current day, last 7 days, and last quarter.
Explain the recommended project structure, data-fetching approach, UI sections, and testing strategy.

Once Bob has responded, scaffold the application:

Create a React application structure for this repository inside a directory named "finance-app".
Include a dashboard page, reusable chart card components, a finance data service layer,
and a clean folder layout suitable for future enhancements.

Observe: Bob creates the finance-app directory with the full project structure.

docs.title: Step 4 — Integrate Yahoo Finance data
docs.text:
Start a + New task in Bob and send:

Implement a finance data layer for the following stock indices using Yahoo Finance data:
Euro Stoxx 50 (`^STOXX50E`), DAX (`^GDAXI`), Nikkei 225 (`^N225`),
Dow Jones Industrial Average (`^DJI`), and MSCI World (`URTH`).
Normalize the returned data so the UI can display quote summaries,
short-term history, and quarterly trend views.
Keep the code easy to extend if more indices need to be added later.

In the same chat, build the dashboard views:

Build 2 to 3 dashboard views for the finance application:
- current day market summary
- last 7 days trend comparison
- last quarter comparison view

Include all five stock indices. Use charts and summary cards. Keep the UI simple and demo-friendly.

Run the app locally to verify:

cd finance-app
npm install
npm start

Why start a new task for each phase?

Bob's context window is 270,000 tokens — large but finite. Each file read, command output, and response consumes budget. Starting a new task with + New task between phases keeps each conversation focused.

Think of it as a clean desk rule: clear yesterday's notes before starting today's work. The planning output is saved to disk (as plan files), not just in the chat, so the implementation task can reference files rather than long conversation history.

docs.title: Step 5 — Add validation and tests
docs.text:
Start a + New task in Bob and send:

Add appropriate validation for the finance dashboard project.
Include unit tests for the data formatting and normalization utilities,
and integration tests for at least one dashboard view rendered with mocked API data.
Use MSW to mock the finance API responses in tests.
Provide a single command that runs lint, type-check, tests, and build together,
and summarize what a successful run looks like.

Run the validation suite:

cd finance-app
npm run validate

A successful run completes without errors — lint, type-check, tests, and build all pass.

Let Bob write the test scaffolding

Asking Bob to provide "a single command that runs lint, type-check, tests, and build together" is a smart delegation. Bob knows the standard npm script conventions and wires up the validate script in package.json. You get a repeatable quality gate without writing a shell wrapper yourself.

docs.title: Step 6 — Push to GitHub
docs.text:
1. Go to https://github.com/new and create a new repo named finance-app (no README, no .gitignore)
  2. Copy the GitHub Actions CI config into your project:
# from the github-sdlc lab root
cp -r .github finance-app/.github
  1. Initialize git and push:
cd finance-app
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit: finance dashboard"
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/finance-app.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
  1. On GitHub, go to Settings → General and confirm Issues is enabled
  2. Create a feature branch:
git checkout -b feature/user-selected-chart
git push -u origin feature/user-selected-chart

Small, frequent commits are the professional pattern

Notice that the initial commit includes everything — but from this point on, each feature should get its own commit. Bob can help: at any time in Agent mode, ask "Commit the changes made so far with a descriptive message." Bob reads your git diff and writes a meaningful commit message automatically.

docs.title: Step 7 — Create a GitHub issue
docs.text:
On GitHub, open Issues → New issue:

  • Title: Add a graph for a user-selected index
  • Body: Users should be able to type any stock ticker symbol and see a new chart for that symbol alongside the existing dashboards. Include loading and error states. Existing dashboard views must not be affected.

Note the issue number (e.g. #1).

Issues as the contract between requester and implementer

Writing a clear issue before implementing is a best practice that makes the automated PR loop much more powerful. When Bob reads the issue via MCP, it has a precise specification — not just a vague description you typed in a chat. The issue becomes the source of truth: referenced in the branch name, referenced in the PR description, closed automatically when the PR merges.

docs.title: Step 8 — Issue-to-PR loop
docs.text:
Open a + New task in Bob (Agent mode) and send — replace #1 with your actual issue number:

Fetch and analyze GitHub issue #1 from this repository.
Explain the requested feature, identify which files need to change,
and propose an implementation plan.

In the same chat, implement:

Implement the feature described in the GitHub issue.
Add a user input for a stock ticker symbol that fetches and displays a new chart
for that symbol alongside the existing dashboards.
Reuse the existing data service layer, keep the UX simple,
and preserve all existing dashboard views.

Validate:

Run the full validation suite. Summarize what passed, what failed,
and whether the branch is ready to push to GitHub.

Start a + New task in Bob, then commit and push:

Review the changes made to implement the user-selected index chart feature in finance-app/.
Summarize what was added, fix any obvious problems, commit with a meaningful message,
and push to the feature/user-selected-chart branch. Do not yet create a pull request.

Why a new task for 'review and commit'?

The implementation task may have left stale reasoning in its context — half-formed plans, earlier error messages, abandoned file reads. Starting a fresh task to review and commit means Bob is reading the final state of the files, not the history of how they were produced. Clean context = accurate review.

docs.title: Step 9 — Create the pull request
docs.text:
In the same chat, type this command directly:

/create-pr

Bob will display a workflow dialog. Click "Start workflow", leave the pre-filled Repository and Base Branch values as-is, then click "Generate PR Description".

Observe: Bob reads the git diff, detects the linked issue, fills in the PR template, and creates the pull request automatically.

What /create-pr does

/create-pr is a built-in Bob slash command that triggers a structured PR workflow. Bob:

  1. Reads the current git diff
  2. Identifies the linked issue from your branch name and commit messages
  3. Generates a PR title and description following your repo's PR template (if one exists)
  4. Creates the PR via GitHub MCP

You review the generated description before it is posted. You are always in the loop.

Check the PR on GitHub

Visit the Pull requests tab on your repo to confirm the PR exists and references the issue number.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
Switch to Ask mode:

In the SDLC loop we just ran, which steps required a human decision
and which were fully automated by Bob?
What are the risks of fully automating the PR step?

Humans stay in the loop by design

Bob's automation is always propose, then approve. You review the implementation plan. You approve each file write. You review the PR description before it posts. The automation handles the mechanical repetition — finding files, writing boilerplate, remembering to reference the issue number — while you focus on the decisions that actually require judgement.

docs.title: Lab I2 — Author, Modify & Commit Rules
docs.text: 30 minutes · Requires Lab I1 complete (git configured)

docs.title: What you will learn
docs.text:
Rules are plain Markdown files that Bob reads before every conversation. They are version-controlled alongside your code and act as always-on team standards — no prompting required.

%%{init: {'theme': 'base', 'themeVariables': {'primaryColor': '#1a56db', 'primaryTextColor': '#ffffff', 'primaryBorderColor': '#1a56db', 'lineColor': '#6b7280', 'mainBkg': '#1a56db', 'nodeBorder': '#1a56db', 'clusterBkg': '#1e3a5f', 'titleColor': '#ffffff', 'edgeLabelBackground': 'transparent'}}}%%
flowchart LR
    R[".bob/rules/\nglobal rules"] --> ALL["All modes"]
    S[".bob/rules-agent/\nmode-scoped rules"] --> AGT["Agent mode only"]
    classDef node fill:#1a56db,color:#fff,stroke:#1a56db
    class R,S,ALL,AGT node

docs.title: Why rules change the development pattern
docs.text:
Without rules, every Bob conversation starts blank. You repeat the same "our project uses X, always do Y" instructions in every prompt. With rules, those standards are injected automatically — enforced at the start of every conversation, in every mode, for every team member.

Rules are a force multiplier:

  • Consistency without supervision — Bob follows the standard even when you forget to mention it
  • Automatic onboarding — new team members get the rules the moment they clone the repo
  • Code-review for standards — rule changes go through your normal PR process, so the team agrees on them before they take effect

docs.title: Step 1 — Create global rules
docs.text:
Open galaxium-travels/ in IBM Bob. In Agent mode:

mkdir -p .bob/rules

Create .bob/rules/01-standards.md with this content:

Always include JSDoc comments for every public function.

Be very concise in responses.

After every Bob interaction, write a summary to the folder `internal-monologue/`.
Name each file with a timestamp prefix followed by a concise description.
Example: 2026-01-15_update-readme.md

Why put rules in .bob/rules/?

Files in .bob/rules/ are global to all modes — they apply whether Bob is in Ask, Plan, or Agent mode. This is the right place for standards that should always be active regardless of what Bob is doing.

The numeric prefix (01-) controls load order. If you have multiple rules files and some should take precedence, use 01-, 02-, etc.

docs.title: Step 2 — Test the rules
docs.text:
In Agent mode, ask Bob to add a utility function:

Add a utility function called formatPrice to
booking_system_frontend/src/services/api.ts
that takes a number and returns a string formatted as "€1,234.56".

Observe:

  • Bob adds the function with a JSDoc comment automatically — because the rule says so
  • A new file appears in internal-monologue/ describing what was changed

This is the value of rules over prompts

You didn't ask for a JSDoc comment. You didn't ask for a summary. Bob did both because the rules told it to. As a team practice, this means code quality standards are enforced without relying on every developer to remember to ask for them.

docs.title: Step 3 — Modify a rule
docs.text:
Edit .bob/rules/01-standards.md — change internal-monologue/ to bob-log/:

After every Bob interaction, write a summary to the folder `bob-log/`.
Name each file with a timestamp prefix followed by a concise description.
Example: 2026-01-15_update-readme.md

Ask Bob to make another small change:

Add a formatDate utility function to the same api.ts file
that formats an ISO date string as "DD MMM YYYY".

Observe: Bob writes to bob-log/ now, not internal-monologue/.

Rules are live — no restart required

Bob reads rules files at the start of each conversation, not at IDE startup. Change a rule, start a new task, and the new rule takes effect immediately. This makes it easy to experiment with different standards before committing them.

docs.title: Step 4 — Add a mode-scoped rule
docs.text:
Create .bob/rules-agent/02-agent-commits.md:

In Agent mode, after every file change create a git commit
with a descriptive message summarising what was changed and why.

Make a small code change in Agent mode (e.g. rename a variable). Observe: Bob commits automatically with a useful message.

Mode-scoped rules

Files in .bob/rules-agent/ are only injected when Bob is in Agent mode. Files in .bob/rules/ are injected in every mode. Mode slug for built-in modes: agent, plan, ask.

This is powerful for compliance. An auto-commit rule in Agent mode means every file Bob touches is committed with a traceable message — a complete audit trail of what Bob did and why, baked into your git history.

docs.title: Step 5 — Commit the rules
docs.text:
git add .bob/ && git commit -m "Add team Bob rules for Galaxium Travels"

Discussion: Why do rules belong in version control alongside the code they govern?

  • New team members get the standards automatically on first git clone
  • Rule changes are reviewed through the normal PR process
  • Rules are scoped to the project, not the developer's global Bob config
  • The full history of what standards were active at any commit is preserved

Rules vs. AGENTS.md — what is the difference?

AGENTS.md .bob/rules/*.md Generated by /init (automated) You (manual) Purpose Describe the project structure Define behaviour standards Edited by Bob + you You (or Bob, on instruction) Example content "This project has a FastAPI backend and a React frontend" "Always use Decimal for monetary values"

Use both together: AGENTS.md tells Bob what the project is, rules tell Bob how to behave in it.

docs.title: Step 6 — Verify the rules persist
docs.text:
Close and reopen IBM Bob, then ask Bob something simple in Agent mode. Check that bob-log/ gets a new entry — confirming the rules survive a session restart.

Rules + AGENTS.md + mode scoping = team Bob configuration

The combination of all three forms a complete Bob configuration for a project:

  1. AGENTS.md — project context (what is this codebase?)
  2. .bob/rules/ — global standards (always apply)
  3. .bob/rules-agent/ — agent-specific behaviour (auto-commit, auto-audit)
  4. .bob/custom_modes.yaml — custom personas (covered in Expert track)

All of it is version-controlled. All of it propagates automatically on git clone. This is what "Bob as a team tool" looks like.
